title: Why was Titicut Follies banned?
summary: Josh and Chuck (credited in the transcript as "iHeart Intro" for Chuck's lines) discuss Frederick Wiseman's 1967 cinema verite documentary Titicut Follies, filmed at Bridgewater State Hospital, a Massachusetts facility for the criminally insane. They cover cinema verite as a style, Wiseman's background as a law professor and filmmaker, the history of Bridgewater from an 1854 almshouse onward, conditions and scenes in the film (including the shaving scene with inmate Jim, Vladimir, and a force-feeding scene), and the legal fight over the film: Lieutenant Governor Elliott Richardson's suppression attempt, Judge Harry Elam Callis's privacy ruling, the ACLU-backed limited-audience compromise, the suicide-related lawsuits, and its eventual release in 1991 under Judge Andrew Gilmeyer. The episode closes with listener mail about effective altruism and a free book offer.

segments.title: Opening banter and Better Things
segments.summary: Hosts open with off-topic banter about Kevin Pollak, the show Better Things, and Project Greenlight.

segments.title: Introducing Titicut Follies and cinema verite
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Titicut Follies as a notorious, disturbing film that is in fact a straightforward cinema verite documentary, and explain the direct cinema style.

segments.title: Cinema verite and early examples
segments.summary: They discuss the minimally intrusive style of cinema verite, Wiseman's view that people act like themselves on camera, and early works by Richard Leacock and Robert Drew such as Mooney Versus Fowler.

segments.title: Documentary recreations
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether re-creations in documentaries work, citing The Kid Stays in the Picture and Forensic Files.
topics: The Kid Stays in the Picture

segments.title: History of Bridgewater State Hospital
segments.summary: Bridgewater began in 1854 as a Massachusetts poorhouse (almshouse) and gradually took in criminals and the mentally ill, becoming the State Asylum for Insane Criminals in 1895 and Bridgewater State Hospital by 1909, later under the Massachusetts Bureau of Prisons.

segments.title: Conditions and civil commitment
segments.summary: Discussion of civil commitment, the lack of medical care (staff saw fewer than half of the 650 men about once a year for about twenty minutes), and the case of Matteo Calicchio, held for decades after a small theft.

segments.title: Frederick Wiseman's background
segments.summary: Wiseman attended Yale law, was drafted for the Korean War, lived in Paris with his wife Zipporah Batshaw, began filmmaking, and was inspired by Shirley Clarke's The Cool World and by taking law students to Bridgewater.

segments.title: Filming permissions and footage
segments.summary: Wiseman obtained permission from the lieutenant governor, the Department of Correction head, and the superintendent, and got consent from the men filmed; he shot over 29 days and typically shoots 75 to 250 hours of footage before editing.

segments.title: Shaving scene and Jim
segments.summary: The hosts describe the forced shaving scene and guards taunting inmate Jim about his room, as well as Jim's later tantrum in his naked cell.

segments.title: Wiseman's approach and the film's raw style
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Wiseman's refusal to editorialize, the available lighting and background noise, and the viewer's sense of witnessing. They compare it to a baseball game without modern extras.

segments.title: Vladimir and the force-feeding scene
segments.summary: The hosts describe Vladimir's lucid plea to be released and clinicians discussing raising his medication, plus Wiseman's regretted force-feeding scene, which he considered ham-fisted.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break before the discussion of the court cases.

segments.title: Legal battle: banning and privacy rulings
segments.summary: Lieutenant Governor Elliott Richardson tried to suppress the film after it premiered, and a 1968 judge Harry Callis found it violated privacy and ordered the negative destroyed. Wiseman appealed; the ruling established a right to privacy in Massachusetts, and the ACLU suggested limiting showings to professionals. The film was shown in film classes, medical schools, and libraries, and suicide-related lawsuits followed.

segments.title: Unbanning and later availability
segments.summary: Wiseman refused to blur faces; a judge later allowed release, and in 1991 Judge Andrew Gilmeyer of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court allowed it to be shown. PBS aired it in 1993, Wiseman sold DVDs, and it streamed on Canopy in 2017. The hosts note ongoing reform issues at Bridgewater and Wiseman's body of work.

segments.title: Effective altruism listener mail
segments.summary: Listener Grace Adams from Giving What We Can offers free books on effective altruism; Toby Ord also wrote in praising the earlier episode.
